facts.text: A detector has four possible outcomes: a true positive reports a real object, a false positive reports an object that is not there, a false negative (or miss) fails to report a real object, and a true negative correctly reports nothing when nothing is there.
facts.quote: it finds something real (true positive), it reports something that is not there (false positive), it misses something real (false negative, or miss), or it correctly stays quiet (true negative).

facts.text: For a braking system, a false negative means the machine does not brake for a person.
facts.quote: A false negative means the machine does not brake for a person.

facts.text: For a braking system, a false positive means braking for nothing, which stops production, shakes the operator and can itself cause an accident.
facts.quote: A false positive means it brakes for nothing, which stops production, shakes the operator and can itself cause an accident

facts.text: Nuisance interventions are the main documented reason deployed systems were rejected or switched off.
facts.quote: nuisance interventions are the main documented reason deployed systems were rejected or switched off [Chapters 4, 8].

facts.text: ISO 21815-3, the international standard for the braking function, acknowledges both false-negative and false-positive errors.
facts.quote: ISO 21815-3, the international standard for this function, acknowledges both kinds [Chapter 9].

facts.text: The booklet distinguishes a false alarm, a warning with no object at all, from a nuisance alarm, a warning for a real object that poses no risk, such as the machine's own tires, a berm or a stockpile.
facts.quote: A false alarm is a warning with no object at all. A nuisance alarm is a warning for a real object that poses no risk, such as the machine's own tires, a berm or a stockpile

facts.text: False alarms and nuisance alarms are different engineering problems and should be counted separately.
facts.quote: these are different engineering problems and should be counted separately [Chapter 7].

facts.text: The booklet's one hard field study recorded 580 alarms over 618 haul-truck reversals: 102 false alarms (18%), 243 nuisance alarms (42%) and 235 alarms requiring action (41%).
facts.quote: In the one hard field study, 580 alarms over 618 reversals of a haul truck split into 102 false (18%), 243 nuisance (42%) and 235 (41%) that required action [Chapter 7].

facts.text: Detection trials should be counted as independent encounters—machine A approaching object B under scenario C—not as sensor frames.
facts.quote: For detection it is the independent encounter, "machine A approached object B under scenario C", not the sensor frame

facts.text: A ten-second detection encounter yields hundreds of correlated sensor frames; treating those frames as independent trials makes confidence intervals artificially narrow.
facts.quote: a ten-second encounter yields hundreds of correlated frames and treating them as trials makes confidence intervals artificially narrow [Chapter 7].

facts.text: Demonstrating at least 95% detection at 95% confidence with no misses requires 59 consecutive successful encounters per condition.
facts.quote: Showing at least 95% detection at 95% confidence with no misses needs 59 consecutive successful encounters per condition

facts.text: Demonstrating 99% detection at 95% confidence with no misses requires 299 consecutive successful encounters per condition.
facts.quote: Showing at least 95% detection at 95% confidence with no misses needs 59 consecutive successful encounters per condition; 99% needs 299 [Chapter 7].

facts.text: False-positive rates should use exposure in hours or maneuvers as the denominator, not staged targets.
facts.quote: For false positives the denominator is exposure, hours or maneuvers, not staged targets

facts.text: Demonstrating fewer than 0.1 false alarms per hour requires at least 30 failure-free hours per condition.
facts.quote: showing fewer than 0.1 false alarms per hour needs at least 30 failure-free hours per condition

facts.text: Event-triggered recording destroys the exposure denominator needed to estimate false-positive rates.
The nuisance-intervention rate should be an acceptance metric equal in weight to missed interventions.
facts.quote: The nuisance-intervention rate should be an acceptance metric equal in weight to missed interventions [Chapter 8].

facts.text: The four detector outcomes underpin every detection and false-alarm claim in the safety case; the outcome being counted determines the booklet's sample sizes and exposure hours.
facts.quote: The four outcomes are the raw material of every detection and false-alarm claim in the safety case, and the booklet's sample sizes and exposure hours follow directly from which box is being counted [Chapters 7, 9].
